titolo: Knight Capital – The 45 Minutes That Destroyed a $440M Company
descrizione:
On August 1, 2012, Knight Capital Group, one of the largest market makers on Wall Street, lost about $440 million in roughly 45 minutes after a faulty software deployment sent millions of unintended orders into the US stock market. This documentary reconstructs what happened using the SEC's October 2013 findings and contemporary reporting.

From a forgotten piece of old code to a missed deployment on one of eight servers, from a rescue deal to a forced merger, we trace how a single technical failure ended an independent company. The video closes with the lessons for software deployment and risk controls.

fatti: Knight Capital Group lost about $440 million on August 1, 2012
The loss happened in roughly 45 minutes after the market opened at 9:30 a.m. ET
Knight was one of the largest US equities market makers, handling a large share of retail order flow
Open loop: how did a routine software update destroy a company, and why could no one stop it
Knight Capital Group was based in Jersey City, New Jersey
In 2012 it was among the largest traders in US equities by volume, per SEC and press reports
It acted as a market maker, buying and selling stocks for brokerages and retail investors
Its market value before the incident was reported at several hundred million dollars, with the stock near $10 before the event
The NYSE launched its Retail Liquidity Program (RLP) on August 1, 2012, with SEC approval
Knight wanted its trading system ready to participate on day one
Knight had to update its order router software, SMARS, before the launch
The SEC found the new code was deployed in the days before August 1
Knight deployed the new code manually to its servers; the SEC found it was installed on only seven of eight servers
The eighth server kept the old code
The new code reused a flag that had once activated an old function called Power Peg
Power Peg was old functionality that had not been used since around 2003; the SEC found it had been left in the system
Knight had no second technician reviewing the deployment, per the SEC findings
Before the open, Knight systems generated 97 automated emails with an error referring to SMARS, per the SEC
The emails were sent to Knight personnel but were not treated as alerts needing immediate action
The SEC found the emails were not designed as system alerts
At the 9:30 a.m. ET open on August 1, 2012, the eighth server began executing the old Power Peg logic
Power Peg kept sending orders because its code to count completed trades no longer worked
The SEC found Knight's system sent over 4 million executions in 154 stocks in roughly 45 minutes
The SEC found that over 397 million shares traded as a result
Reports noted abnormal price moves in many of the affected stocks
Knight engineers struggled to identify the cause during the incident
They rolled back the new code on the seven servers, which the SEC found made the problem worse
The rollback caused the flag to activate Power Peg on all eight servers
Trading was finally stopped around 10:15 a.m. ET
Knight ended with a large unwanted position of about $7 billion in stock, per the SEC and press reports
The SEC cited a loss of about $460 million; Knight reported about $440 million pretax in company statements
Knight's stock fell about 33% on August 1, 2012 and about 63% over two days after the incident
On August 6, 2012, Knight announced a $400 million financing from a group of investors
The investors included Jefferies, Blackstone, Getco, Stephens, Stifel and TD Ameritrade
The financing was in the form of convertible preferred stock
In December 2012, Getco agreed to merge with Knight, and the combined company became KCG Holdings in July 2013
In October 2013, the SEC charged Knight with violating the Market Access Rule (Rule 15c3-5)
Knight agreed to pay a $12 million penalty without admitting or denying the findings
The SEC found Knight lacked adequate controls and procedures for the code deployment
Lessons: dead code should be removed, deployments need automation and verification, alerts need clear ownership, and kill switches need to exist
Answer to the loop: a single server running old code, plus no safeguards, erased Knight's independence in 45 minutes
Ending line: Subscribe for the next one.
